events.ai_basis: The vast majority of results were obtained with the same procedure using an unreleased internal OpenAI model.

why: The statement asks for a uniform μ(λ) for all AECs with LS(K) ≤ λ in ZFC. The OpenAI manuscript (6 October 2026) claims exactly this, with a uniform threshold and no extra hypotheses, so I scored it whole. It is unreviewed: the Lean build covers only the companion CH-obstruction result, not the categoricity theorem (F7). I scored it credible because the only thing against it is that it is eight days old and unreviewed, and F10 says that alone is not a reason for doubt. Its AI role is generated: the README credits the model with producing the results, and the repository names no human authors. Espíndola's v7 also claims the whole conjecture, but it predates the snapshot. I scored it doubtful because of scope growth between versions, an SCH dependence and a non-uniform threshold. Results that need large cardinals, weak GCH, amalgamation, tameness, primes or universal classes are cases. Results whose hypotheses change the question are variants: cofinality-based categoricity, two-cardinal downward transfer, categoricity spectra, the L_{ω1,ω} sibling problem, and the namesake Hanf-number conjecture. Boney, Vasey and Shelah–Vasey are digested through journals of record.
doubts: Close call: whether the OpenAI claim should be doubtful rather than credible. It is a landmark claim that its own record says contrasts with decades of conditional results. The researcher did not read its core sections (02–13), including the set-coding reduction behind the uniform form. The record also does not say whether the manuscript addresses Espíndola's prior ZFC claim. Placing conditional-on-axiom results (strongly compact cardinals, GCH plus a measurable cardinal) as 'case' rather than 'variant' is a judgement call, but it does not change anything after the snapshot.
